If you know anything about Vikings other than that they raided European towns and monasteries from the late 8th century, then it is thanks in large part to the rich tradition of medieval Icelandic literature, especially the sagas. The Icelandic noun saga is from the verb Sägia, meaning to speak or to say, because in olden times the only evening entertainment in Iceland, especially during the long harsh winter, was to gather around the fire and listen to someone reciting or reading the ancient stories of the land and the people, the sagas. In the written form they survive today, the 40 or so Icelandic sagas are a product of the 13th and 14th centuries when they were put to paper, but they are mostly set in the Viking period between the settling of Iceland in the 9th century up until the 11th century, and this is when many of the stories were originally composed in oral form. While the rest of literate Europe was obsessed with medieval romance such as the stories of King Arthur, Iceland had preserved a unique type of literature derived from native oral traditions. They are mostly realistic accounts of events with a typically Nordic style of Laconic prose, which avoids flowery language but subtly alludes to events which it does not mention directly. The themes are those which concerned men of the Viking Age, honor, vengeance, blood feuds, paganism and Christianity.
